content: The results of the search were presented in a flow diagram following PRISMA guidelines. Data extraction and management were conducted independently by three authors to minimize bias. Data were verified by an independent reviewer for accuracy and completeness, with disagreements resolved through discussion. The NOS uses a star system to judge studies on three perspectives: This tool avoids unreliable pooled scores and is specifically designed for non-randomized studies. The literature search across databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, and EMBASE) identified 651 potentially relevant publications. After screening titles and abstracts, 167 references were retrieved in full text, with an additional 14 identified through reference checking. Approximately 40 cohort groups were identified, of which 15 were well-established. Evidence was available from 31 studies conducted in high-income countries and nine studies from lowand middle-income countries. The identified cohorts included notable studies such as the Helsinki Birth Cohort (Finland), Aberdeen Children of the 1950s Study (UK), Norwegian Cohort (Norway), Danish Birth Cohort (Denmark), and the Bogalusa Heart Study (USA), among others. From lowand middle-income countries, cohorts included the New Delhi Birth Cohort (India), Pelotas Birth Cohort (Brazil), and Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (Philippines). The quality assessment of included studies varied, with most scoring high for sample selection but showing variability in comparability. BMI tracking data from 28 studies (40,219 individuals) showed significant trends, with high childhood BMI associated with increased obesity risk in later life. Similar trends were observed across highand low-income countries. Thirteen studies demonstrated that high childhood or adolescent BMI was linked to a higher risk of obesity in adulthood. Rapid weight gain during infancy and childhood was a strong predictor of later obesity. Height status also showed similar associations. These studies included coronary heart disease (CHD), ischemic heart disease, and stroke. Findings varied, with some studies showing significant associations between high childhood BMI and increased CVD risk, while others found no significant relationship. For example, the Helsinki Birth Cohort found that lower childhood BMI followed by rapid weight gain increased CHD risk. Conversely, the Danish study showed a positive association between childhood BMI and CHD. Carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT), a marker of subclinical atherosclerosis, was studied in 14 articles (nine cohorts). Most studies found a positive association between childhood BMI and adult cIMT levels, though some relationships were attenuated after adjusting for adult BMI. For instance, the New Delhi Birth Cohort found that rapid weight gain in childhood increased cIMT levels, but this was mitigated by adjusting for adult waist circumference. Regarding type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), pooled analyses from British birth cohorts and other high-income countries demonstrated that obesity in adulthood, combined with overweight in earlier life, significantly increased T2DM risk. However, being overweight only during childhood or adolescence did not increase T2DM risk. Rapid BMI increases during childhood and adolescence were strong predictors of T2DM in adulthood. These findings emphasize the importance of early-life interventions to mitigate adverse health outcomes later in life.
